Note · Rumelt — Good Strategy / Bad Strategy

3 min read796 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-rumelt-good-strategy.md

Canon · Cluster: Strategy · Maps to Course 04 (Competitive Strategy), Course 12 (Capstone)

  • Source: Richard Rumelt, Good Strategy Bad Strategy (2011)
  • Core claim: Most "strategy" is bad strategy — goals dressed up as strategy, or a list of priorities that aren't prioritized. Strategy is problem-solving, not aspiration.
  • Framework — the kernel (3 parts): 1. Diagnosis — name what's actually going on; identify the single most critical challenge. 2. Guiding policy — the overall approach you're choosing to meet that challenge. 3. Coherent action — steps that reinforce each other (not a scattered to-do list).
  • "Bad strategy" = fluff (restating the obvious) + failure to make hard choices.
  • Applies when: you face a complex, ambiguous challenge and need to focus finite energy against the one thing that matters most. The diagnosis step is where almost everyone cheats.
  • Breaks when: the "single critical challenge" framing tempts oversimplification — some situations have two genuinely coupled constraints, and forcing one diagnosis loses the other. Also: a brilliant kernel still dies in execution if intent isn't transmitted downward (see canon bungay art of action). And diagnosis is only as good as your systems-model of the problem (canon meadows thinking in systems) — a wrong diagnosis is confidently wrong.
  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-05 — r/strategy corpus + Lenny's Podcast / Rumelt transcripts) The corpus confirms Rumelt's core complaint and complicates it. r/strategy practitioners repeatedly describe the exact "fluff" failure: a high-traffic "Most organizations don't need a new strategy" thread (45↑) argues most "strategy refreshes" are misdiagnosed — "the strategy isn't broken — the communication and operating rhythm are" (priorities shifting, KPIs tracked but never reviewed, "meetings full of updates but short on decisions"). A "Leaders who run strategy workshops" thread (27↑) lists the same rot from the inside: "Bad strategy that good execution won't fix" and "good ideas don't turn into action." But the recurring pushback is that diagnosis isn't where most teams actually fail — execution and alignment are. Rumelt half-concedes this himself: "organizational Dynamics are often the biggest hindrance to winning strategies" — which is why the corpus keeps pointing past the kernel toward canon bungay art of action.

  • The discipline that defines it: deciding what you will not do.

  • Researched layer (2026-06-05)

  • Canonical explanation (sourced): Rumelt insists strategy is "a design for overcoming a high-stakes challenge… a mixture of policy and action designed to deal with a challenge" — not a goal, mission, or vision. He'd rather you "don't call it a strategy, call it an action agenda" (Lenny's Podcast). The work itself is diagnosis first: "part of what a diagnosis is is a decision of what you're going to pay attention to" — naming the one or two key challenges, then choosing a guiding policy and coherent actions to attack them.
  • The kernel, verified across transcripts: the explainer "What IS Strategy? (No Fluff!)" walks the same three parts — "diagnosis defines WHY, the guiding policy defines WHAT, coherent actions explain HOW" — and catalogs Rumelt's four flavors of bad strategy: fluff (the real bank line "Our fundamental strategy is one of customer-centric intermediation"), failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals/vision for strategy, and bad strategic objectives.
  • Real application (mined): the transcript's worked case is Blockbuster vs. Netflix — Blockbuster "didn't really understand the challenge and just launched a few online services without a real analysis of the commitments and investments required." It's a textbook missed diagnosis: a guiding-policy reflex (add a channel) bolted onto a problem nobody had named.
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: r/strategy practitioners argue the binding constraint is usually downstream of the kernel. The "Most organizations don't need a new strategy" thread (45↑) and the "Leaders who run strategy workshops" thread (27↑) both locate failure in alignment, operating rhythm, and execution — "good ideas don't turn into action," "bad execution that good strategy won't fix (more likely)." A clean kernel is necessary but not sufficient; transmitting intent downward is the part Rumelt's three boxes under-weight (hence canon bungay art of action).
  • Sources in corpus: Lenny's Podcast — "Good Strategy, Bad Strategy | Richard Rumelt" (youtube.com/watch?v=4uWKEG0s9Kc) · "What IS Strategy? (No Fluff!)" (vyezDs2KCAE) · r/strategy "Most organizations don't need a new strategy" (45↑), "Leaders who run strategy workshops — what's harder than it should be?" (27↑), "Playing to Win (one paragraph review)" (102↑).

Rep

Take your employer's current "strategy." Strip it to a kernel: write the one-sentence diagnosis, the guiding policy, and 3 coherent actions. Notice how much was fluff.

Marks itself read when you reach the end.
